Recent research supports separating recency sensitivity from order sensitivity. [Oh and Cho (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) propose measuring recency bias and report that excessive recency emphasis can hurt recommendation accuracy. [Liu et al. (RecSys 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) show that arbitrary history shuffling confounds user sequence patterns with item availability; constrained shuffling respects items’ first appearances. Thus, perturbation sensitivity alone does not establish causal user intent. [BERT4Rec’s original formulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690) requires masked-target training to prevent bidirectional target leakage.

Suggested diagnostic design, synthesized from these findings: use paired training-history prefixes with identical targets and fixed candidates; compare recent deletions against equal-count random deletions matched on item frequency, and permute earlier items while preserving the latest item. Report paired changes in target rank, score margin and top-10 overlap. Include deterministic identity controls and deliberately injected wrong-readout/MASK faults to verify probe sensitivity; for left padding, explicitly check the final nonpadding readout. Bootstrap users within category, retaining all prefixes from each sampled user together, then macro-average category effects. These controls are proposed engineering checks, not a validated protocol established by the cited papers.

[ Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) show sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation. Keep the host’s fixed 99-negative validation HR@10 unchanged; describe it as candidate-set performance. Any full-catalog unseen-item ranking diagnostics should be reported separately, without interpreting sampled HR@10 as full-catalog retrieval quality.
